opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a very different job from a traditional product manager, and a lot of people haven't fully absorbed that yet.

In the traditional internet era, the product manager's core skill was understanding user needs and then designing a flow, a set of buttons and pages, that the engineers could build. The technology was relatively stable. You knew what a database could do, what a mobile phone could do, so the question was mainly "what should we build for people?"

With AI, the capability frontier is moving every few months. So a good AI product manager first needs a real, hands-on intuition for what the models can and can't do right now, and where they're likely to be in six months or a year. Not from reading papers secondhand, but from actually using the models a lot, poking at them, seeing where they break. If you design a product around today's limitations, there's a good chance the next model release makes your whole design irrelevant. If you design for a capability that's still two years away, you'll ship something that doesn't work. So part of the job is timing: sensing which capabilities are just about to cross the threshold of being useful.

The second thing is that a lot of the value now comes from how you define the task and the environment, rather than how you design the interface. When the model is the agent doing the work, the product question becomes: what context does it have, what tools can it use, how does it get feedback, and how does the user stay in the loop and trust it? That's closer to research thinking. You're designing the setup where intelligence can actually be useful, not just a UI wrapped around a fixed function.

And third, I'd say taste and imagination matter more than before. The default thing people do is take an existing workflow and add a chatbot to it. But the really interesting products probably look like new forms of interaction we don't have names for yet. Someone who can imagine "if the model can now do X reliably, what becomes possible that wasn't possible before?" and then work backwards from that, I think that's what makes a great AI product person.

So in a way, the boundary between researcher and product manager is getting blurrier. The best people I've seen understand both the model and the human, and can move back and forth between them.

r001.rationale: The response says AI capabilities move every few months and contrasts this with stable technology in the traditional internet era, but it does not state that human needs change more slowly than AI technology.

r002.rationale: It describes understanding user needs in traditional product management and imagining products from new model capabilities, but does not recommend choosing technologies by reasoning backward from a human need.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't fully know yet, because the role is still being invented. But I can tell you what I think the key shift is.

Traditional product management is mostly about understanding users and translating that into specifications for engineers. The product behavior is deterministic, so your job is really about judgment on what to build, and then the engineers build it. With AI products, especially agents, the boundary between what the product is and what the model is becomes blurry. The model has its own capabilities and its own failure modes, and those change every few months. So a good AI PM has to have real intuition about the model itself, not just about the user.

Concretely, I think there are three things. First, you need to actually use the models a lot, on hard things, so you develop a feel for where the frontier is. Not in a demo sense, but in a daily-work sense. If you don't know what the model can almost do, you'll either build something that's already trivially solved or something that's two years too early. Second, you need to think in terms of evaluation rather than features. In classic software you ship a feature and it works or it doesn't. With AI the question is always, how good is it, in what distribution of cases, and how do we measure that. The PM who can define what "good" means for a task, in a way you can actually measure, is enormously valuable, because that definition drives the whole training and iteration loop. It's really the same skill as designing a benchmark.

And third, I think you need some humility about timing. A lot of product work in AI gets obsoleted by the next model. So the question is not just "is this useful today," but "is this a product that gets better as the model gets better, or one that gets replaced." The good PMs I've seen are the ones who bet on the model improving and build the scaffolding, the interface, the data flywheel around that, rather than patching over today's weaknesses with a lot of hand-engineering.

So maybe the short version is: a good AI PM is half a researcher. They need taste about users, like any PM, but they also need taste about models. And the people who have both are very rare right now.

r002.rationale: It discusses understanding users and evaluating AI products, but does not recommend choosing technologies by reasoning backward from a human need.

astra-6.text:
I think a good AI product manager needs to understand both what users want and what the technology can actually do. And the difficult part is that both of those are uncertain. Users might ask for a chatbot, but what they really want is to finish a task. Meanwhile, a model can look very impressive in a demo and still fail often enough that people won’t trust it in their daily work.

So I’d look for someone who can turn an ambiguous need into a concrete task: What information does the AI need? What actions can it take? What does success look like? When should it ask the user for help? You don’t necessarily need to train models yourself, but you should be able to experiment with them and understand their failure modes.

And then you need good judgment about how the product should evolve. If you build everything around today’s limitations, a better model might make your work irrelevant. But if you assume the next model will solve everything, you may never deliver something useful today. The challenge is to solve a real problem now while leaving room for the technology to improve.

For me, the strongest signal would be someone who builds a small version, watches people use it, examines where it fails, and learns quickly. In AI, that feedback loop matters much more than having a very confident story about the future.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses uncertainty in user needs and AI capabilities, but does not say that human needs change more slowly than AI technology.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting with the real user problem, translating it into a concrete task, and then identifying what the AI needs to do.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a good AI product manager needs two kinds of judgment: understanding what users actually need, and understanding what the technology can reliably do. The interesting opportunities are where those two meet.

With AI, you can build a demo that looks amazing but fails in everyday use. So you need to ask: What does success look like for this task? How often does the system succeed? What happens when it makes a mistake? Sometimes the most important product decision is choosing a narrower problem where the model is already useful.

You also need to be willing to revise your assumptions. The models keep changing, so something that required a complicated workflow six months ago might become much simpler. But the user's underlying problem may stay the same. I would look for someone who can experiment with the technology, learn from users, and distinguish an impressive capability from a product people will keep using.

r001.rationale: It says models keep changing while the user’s underlying problem may stay the same, conveying that human needs change more slowly than AI technology.

r002.rationale: It connects understanding user needs with what technology can reliably do and recommends choosing a narrower problem where the model is useful, conveying that product choices should start from the human need.
